paras: The attempted lynching of Robert Wilson took place in Memphis, Tennessee, in the early hours of October 2, 1882, when a crowd of about 200 to 250 people gathered at the Shelby County jail and demanded Wilson, a 19-year-old Black prisoner accused of fatally shooting a grocer. The jailer refused to give up the keys and the crowd dispersed, and Wilson was later convicted of murder and sentenced to hang. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a failed lynching by a crowd that lacked a leader, while a Memphis daily openly regretted the failure.

On the night of September 28, 1882, grocer Frank B. Russell saw Wilson leaving his store at Hernando and Vance streets with a bucket of lard, chased him, shot him in the leg, and took him prisoner. According to the Memphis Daily Appeal, Russell took Wilson into W. B. Safford's drug store to dress the wound, where a struggle followed and Russell was shot in the abdomen and breast. Police Captain Hackett arrested Wilson in bed at his house on Pontotoc street early the next morning, together with a man named Wm. Hunt.

While Russell lay dying, the Memphis Public Ledger wrote that Wilson "trembles with fear lest an outraged people should take his case in hand," and asked in its column of questions how "a vigilance committee" would do for the thief who shot Russell. A crowd gathered on Saturday night, September 30, intending to hang Wilson, but decided against it because Russell was still alive.

Russell died about seven o'clock on the evening of Sunday, October 1, and within an hour a hundred or more men lined the sidewalk in front of his house. Between 1 and 2 a.m., by the Public Ledger's account, about two hundred people collected in front of the county jail, and several masked men advanced to the gate and demanded the keys. The jailer, William Quinn, refused, and after a short parley the crowd dispersed; the Ledger said the movement was "desultory and wholly unorganized." The wire version put the crowd at 250 and the hour at "late" Sunday night, and said it loitered about the jail for an hour without further demonstration.

No report of arrests among the crowd appears in the coverage. Wilson was indicted for murder on October 6, and on October 26 Sheriff Athy brought him back to Memphis from Nashville, where he had been held. On December 4 a Criminal Court jury of nine white and three Black men convicted him of first-degree murder after about thirty minutes.

On December 9 Judge Horrigan denied a new trial and sentenced Wilson to hang on February 3, 1883, and the Appeal expected an appeal to the April term of the Supreme Court to delay the execution until about June. The coverage does not show the result of the appeal.

The Public Ledger took the strongest line, calling Wilson a "vile scoundrel" and remarking that had he stayed in the "insecure stationhouse" his "carcass would by this time adorn a lamp post." Five days later its column of questions asked, "How would Robert Wilson's carcass look on a lamp post?" The Memphis Daily Appeal reported "considerable talk of lynching" and that many thought no trial necessary, but called the leaderless gathering a "farce."

Outside Tennessee, a short Memphis dispatch ran on October 3 in the Washington Evening Star, the St. Paul Daily Globe and both Wheeling dailies. Its headlines treated the episode with ridicule, among them "Lacked the Necessary Sand," "Didn't Get Him" and "A Lynching Party That Failed," and the Globe ran it directly after a report of a jail lynching at Charlottesville, Virginia. Wilson was identified only as "a negro" in the wire, which reported the crowd's demand without comment on its legality.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Wilson
bases: Crowds gathered to hang Robert Wilson, a Black prisoner accused of killing a white grocer, and about 200-250 went to the Shelby County jail and demanded him, dispersing without taking him (A4, A5, A9).

A crowd of about 200-250 demanded Wilson from the jail to hang him for the killing of Russell, but the jailer refused and the crowd dispersed; Wilson was not harmed and was later tried, convicted and sentenced by a court (A4, A5, A17). It is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
Two Memphis dailies reported the jail crowd independently (A4, A9), and a separate Memphis wire report carried in several papers agrees on the core event (A5, A6, A7).

accounts.label: Memphis Public Ledger (local)
accounts.gist: About two hundred gathered at the jail between 1 and 2 a.m.; masked men demanded the keys, the jailer refused, and the crowd dispersed 'for want of a leader'; a Saturday-night crowd had held off because Russell was still alive.

accounts.label: Memphis wire report
accounts.gist: A crowd of 250 went to the jail late Sunday night and demanded Bob Wilson, loitered an hour without further demonstration, and evidently needed a leader.

accounts.label: Memphis Daily Appeal (local)
accounts.gist: Amid 'considerable talk of lynching,' a crowd assembled near the jail Sunday night but nobody took the lead and the enterprise 'proved a farce.'

framing.detail: The Public Ledger called Wilson a 'vile scoundrel,' said his 'carcass would by this time adorn a lamp post' had he stayed in the stationhouse, and asked how a vigilance committee would do and how his carcass would look on a lamp post.
The Appeal reported that many thought 'there is no necessity for a trial' and called the leaderless crowd a 'farce.'
Out-of-town papers ran the wire under mocking heads such as 'Lacked the Necessary Sand,' 'Didn't Get Him,' 'Needed a Leader' and 'A Lynching Party That Failed.'

conflicts.note: Probably the same night described two ways; the Ledger's local, same-day hour is the more precise.
